lesson.title: Hashing, passwords and authentication
lesson.subtitle: Salts, slow hashes and second factors

video.title: Hashing, passwords and authentication: Salts, slow hashes and second factors

scenes.narration: A student project stored passwords as plain SHA two fifty six hashes. When the table leaked in a class exercise, a laptop recovered half of them in an afternoon.
Today: what a cryptographic hash guarantees, why passwords need salted slow hashes, and where a second factor really helps.

A cryptographic hash maps any input to a short fixed-length digest. It should be infeasible to find an input from a digest, or two inputs with the same digest. Change one bit, and the digest changes completely.
General hashes are designed to be fast. A graphics card can try billions of guesses a second. People choose predictable passwords, so an attacker hashes a dictionary and looks for matches.
Here is the relative rate of guesses on one graphics card. A plain fast hash allows vastly more guesses than a slow, memory-hard function tuned to take a tenth of a second per login.

Store passwords with a unique random salt per user and a slow function such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon two. The salt stops precomputed tables and makes identical passwords look different. The cost factor slows every guess.

A second factor means a stolen password alone is not enough. One-time codes help against reuse, but can still be phished. Hardware keys bound to the site's address resist phishing, because they will not sign for a fake domain.
Quick check! Two users have the same password. With a unique salt each, what do their stored hashes look like?
Different. So an attacker cannot spot shared passwords, and must attack each one separately. A precomputed table for one salt is useless for the next.
In the app, open the hash lab. Change one letter of the input and compare the digests, then add a salt and watch identical passwords diverge.
Your turn. A staff member typed a password and a one-time code into a fake login page. Which second factor would have stopped the attacker?
A hardware security key bound to the real site. Remember: fast hashes are wrong for passwords, salt every user, tune a slow function, and prefer phishing-resistant factors.

checkpoints.prompt: Two users share a password. With a unique salt each, their stored hashes are:

options.text: Identical until the cost factor is raised

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: salts make each hash unique, so each password must be attacked separately.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: the salt is part of the input, so the same password gives different hashes.

checkpoints.prompt: A fake page relayed a password and one-time code to the real site at once. Which second factor would have stopped it?

options.text: A push prompt to approve the sign-in

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the key won't sign for the fake domain.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a code or a push approval can be relayed in real time; only an origin-bound key refuses a fake site.
